title: Given a set of numbers that may contain duplicates, generate all possible unique subsets, with no two subsets identical. Explain how sorting plus a controlled expansion of only the newly added subsets prevents duplicate subsets.
shortTitle: Subsets With Duplicates (Generate Unique Subsets When Elements Repeat)

s1_definition.profdef: Subsets With Duplicates generates every distinct subset when the input contains repeated elements. We first sort the input so equal elements are adjacent. We then use iterative doubling, but when the current element equals the previous element, we only extend the subsets created in the previous round, not all subsets, which prevents producing the same subset twice. The work is proportional to the number of distinct subsets produced.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's available cashback coupons may include duplicates, like two identical five-percent coupons. When we enumerate every distinct coupon bundle, choosing the first five-percent coupon or the second must not count as two different bundles. We sort the coupons so identical ones sit together, and when we process a repeat we only grow the bundles that received the previous identical coupon, which stops us from generating the same bundle twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort first, and for a repeated element extend only the subsets added in the previous round to avoid duplicate subsets.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Subsets With Duplicates generates every distinct subset when the input contains repeated elements. We first sort the input so equal elements are adjacent. We then use iterative doubling, but when the current element equals the previous element, we only extend the subsets created in the previous round, not all subsets, which prevents producing the same subset twice. The work is proportional to the number of distinct subsets produced.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's available cashback coupons may include duplicates, like two identical five-percent coupons. When we enumerate every distinct coupon bundle, choosing the first five-percent coupon or the second must not count as two different bundles. We sort the coupons so identical ones sit together, and when we process a repeat we only grow the bundles that received the previous identical coupon, which stops us from generating the same bundle twice.

**One line to remember:** Sort first, and for a repeated element extend only the subsets added in the previous round to avoid duplicate subsets.

sections.s2_technical:
Sorting places equal values next to each other, which is the precondition for the duplicate-skip rule. We track the start index into the subsets list where the previous round began. For a fresh, non-duplicate element we extend all existing subsets, as in the plain subsets problem. For an element equal to the previous one we extend only the subsets from `startIndex` to the end of the list, which are exactly the ones that gained the previous identical element.

For example, we compute `int start = (num == previous) ? previousRoundStart : 0;` and then iterate `for (int i = start; i < size; i++)` copying and extending. We update `previousRoundStart` to the size before this round each time. This surgical restriction is what avoids over-counting.

A senior-level nuance is why extending only the previous round is correct: a new copy of a duplicate value must attach to subsets that already contain the earlier copy, otherwise we would create a subset with one copy that is indistinguishable from one produced earlier. Another nuance is that without sorting the adjacency assumption breaks, so sorting is not optional here.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India issues Rajesh a basket of cashback coupons that can include identical duplicates, and marketing wants every distinct coupon bundle for display. Treating two identical coupons as distinct would flood the list with duplicate bundles. This is exactly how Subsets With Duplicates works: it enumerates only distinct subsets.

Problem 2 — The naive doubling approach would generate the same bundle multiple times when coupons repeat. This is why we sort the coupons and, on a repeated coupon, extend only the bundles from the previous round, producing each distinct bundle exactly once.

The code defines a `DupSubsetsService` exposing `distinctBundles(coupons)` returning distinct coupon-value lists. A `Demo` runs it over coupons that include a duplicate and logs the distinct bundles.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: coupons 5, 5, 10. After sorting they stay 5, 5, 10.

Step 1: Start with the empty bundle, list is [[]].

Step 2: First coupon 5 is new. Extend all existing subsets, adding [5]. List becomes [[], [5]]. Record that this round started at index 1.

Step 3: Second coupon 5 equals the previous 5, so extend only the subsets from the previous round start, which is index 1, the single [5]. Adding 5 gives [5, 5]. List becomes [[], [5], [5, 5]]. We did not re-extend the empty bundle, which would have produced a duplicate [5].

Step 4: Coupon 10 is new. Extend all three existing subsets, adding 10 to each. List becomes [[], [5], [5, 5], [10], [5, 10], [5, 5, 10]].

Step 5: The six distinct bundles contain no repeats, correctly treating the two 5s as interchangeable.

    │ + 5 (new) extend all → add [5]

sections.s6_takeaway:
Subsets With Duplicates generates every distinct subset when the input may contain repeated elements, and the challenge is to avoid producing the same subset twice. I first sort the input so that equal elements sit next to each other, which is a hard precondition for the technique. Then I use iterative doubling, but with one rule: when the current element equals the previous element, I extend only the subsets created in the previous round rather than all existing subsets. For a brand-new element I extend everything as usual.

The reason this works is that a second copy of a duplicate value must attach only to subsets that already contain the first copy. If I extended all subsets, I would attach the second copy to subsets that have no copy, producing a subset indistinguishable from one I already made with the first copy. Restricting the expansion to the previous round's subsets produces each distinct subset exactly once.

At the National Bank of India I used this to enumerate distinct cashback-coupon bundles for a customer like Rajesh, whose basket could contain identical coupons, so marketing needed each real bundle listed once rather than duplicated by which identical coupon was chosen. I sorted the coupons, extended only the previous round on repeats, and produced clean distinct bundles. Explaining the sort precondition and the previous-round-only expansion is what tells an interviewer that I understand precisely how the Subsets pattern is adapted to handle duplicates.
